session01.section: Introduction and Section 10.7; PDF pages 1–2 and 34–35
session01.purpose: Names the six LLM research applications and distinguishes exact replay from claim-level replication while specifying a minimum research record.
Provides a social-science framework for measurement, prompting and simulation.
Shows how generative AI is entering sociological research and where disciplinary judgment remains necessary.
Turns general transparency concerns into fields a researcher can actually save.
Explains why model access and versioning complicate conventional replication.

session02.purpose: Introduces annotation, validation and the weakening of an unquestioned human gold standard.
Connects established coding decisions to prompt design.
Treats semantically similar prompt variants as a reliability problem.
Locates zero-shot classification among other ways of adapting a model.
Connects annotation performance to downstream social-science use.

session03.purpose: Establishes abductive analysis as movement between surprising observations and alternative theoretical accounts.
Shows a researcher–LLM–researcher process for qualitative coding.
Applies comparative life-history analysis to different pathways into high-risk mobilization.
Makes the chatbot interaction itself part of the methodological account.
Provides a recent empirical case in which humans retained the interpretive analysis.

session04.purpose: Shows how professional communities organize what becomes visible as evidence.
Explains how video sequence analysis turns recorded action into analyzable data.
Applies sequence analysis to confrontation, tension and emotional entrainment in violent situations.
Introduces the technical debate over what text-only models lack about embodied experience.

session05.purpose: Places generated vignettes within the sociology of factorial survey design.
Compares human-written, LLM-generated and human-selected LLM messages in experiments with human participants.
Applies framing theory in an experiment on support for immigrant rights.
Explains why two differently worded treatments may change more than the intended construct.
Shows how candidate questions can be selected adaptively without treating generation as validation.

session06.purpose: Asks when interview accounts can support claims about situated action and shows why talk and observed conduct may diverge.
Combines a semi-structured LLM interview with an experiment in which the conversation determines which personalized counterargument a participant can receive.
Provides a major contemporary implementation of AI-led interviews.
Uses interviews and observation to explain how evaluators construct cultural fit in elite hiring.
Shows how a qualitative chatbot was built and how researchers experienced it.
Provides the classic criteria of nondirection, specificity, range, depth and personal context for focused interviewing.
Provides a comparison in which participant contributions change a shared question bank across respondents rather than the next probe within one interview.

session07.purpose: Documents the Simulmatics attempt to turn archived polls into a computational electorate during the 1960 campaign.
Builds interview-grounded agents for 1,052 people and evaluates their held-out predictions against human test-retest consistency.
Tests how generative models answer survey questions and where their distributions differ.
Provides a broader sociological framework for deciding what an artificial stand-in would need to preserve.
Keeps human observations as the reference data and uses LLM predictions only when they measurably improve precision.
Tests whether demographic and interview-grounded personas improve distributional fidelity for the same observed respondents.
Uses the history of Simulmatics to ask who constructs, queries and acts on a computational public.

session08.purpose: Uses observed survey answers to predict missing responses for actual respondents.
Separates resemblance on one statistic from broader population realism.
Applies multilevel regression and poststratification to state opinion and studies policy responsiveness on gay rights.
Tests prediction of experimental results rather than replacement of individual participants.
Trains and evaluates one model across 160 cognitive experiments, including held-out tasks and altered contexts.
Provides a hard case for claims that missing social worlds have been recovered.

session09.purpose: Shows how the same CT scanner became part of different occupational relations in two hospitals.
Estimates changes in measured customer-support performance while workers had access to an LLM assistant.
Separates performance during AI-assisted data-science tasks from technical knowledge tested without ChatGPT afterward.
Places LLM recommendations within the longer development of algorithmic control at work.
Examines emotional demands and repair work that productivity measures may omit.
Shows why access to AI can help or harm performance depending on the task.
Distinguishes individual time savings from changes that require organizational coordination.
Locates the outsourced human labour required to build and maintain systems described as automated.
